paper_title: ChronoReplay: One Answer Interface Is Not Enough for Streaming Spatial Intelligence

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Training a spatial VLM to answer which side an object lies on does not require it to preserve the metric displacement that determines that answer, while supervision for a distance estimate may leave categorical relations largely unconstrained. When post-training emphasizes one readout, improvements can therefore concentrate on that interface while transfer to others remains weak or even degrades; we call this observed specialization interface lock-in. ChronoReplay addresses it by replaying heterogeneous spatial supervision as chronologically ordered episodes, retaining source-native targets, and balancing supervision across families. Under the same observation access, a single ChronoReplay checkpoint improves OVO-S-Bench, OST-Bench, and UCS-Bench together, including a 13.41-point gain on OST-Bench, and achieves the highest three-benchmark mean among the supervision settings compared here. Same-data controls further separate the ingredients of this transfer: answer serialization redistributes gains across OST and UCS, family-balanced learning improves over ordinary joint SFT and natural turn weighting, and chronological replay exceeds a shifted-order control by about 2.41 OST points across two paired seeds. Adaptive frame selection then changes evidence access while keeping the trained model fixed, providing an additional inference-time gain at lower visual cost. Streaming spatial performance depends on what distinctions supervision preserves, how heterogeneous histories are organized during learning, and what causal evidence inference makes available at test time.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: A home robot follows you through your apartment and is later asked: Is the mirror on my left or right? How far is the sofa from here? When did we pass the plant? One walk, three questions, three answer forms: an option, number in meters, moment in time. Answering them from video stream means associating objects across views, accumulating the observers motion, and recovering relations in changing reference frames [37, 48, 53, 63, 65], using only what was observed before the question; streaming spatial benchmarks now pose all three over one causal history. Recent progress comes from two directions. Architectural work retains the stream with visual memories, bounded caches, fast weights, maps, and scene graphs [15, 29, 43, 46]; data work post-trains VLMs on spatial instruction data [59, 62, 64]. Both are typically single-interface: recipe supervises one answer format and reports the benchmark that shares it; even recipes that mix qualitative and metric questions [7, 11] train on single images, so whether one model can serve categorical, metric, and temporal queries over the same causal history is untested. Building on this, we show that changing the supervision can achieve this without new memory module or new annotation. 1 Figure 1: Why reusable spatial state. Categorical preservation and trajectory supervision constrain complementary spatial distinctions. Causal Replay combines them in shared parameters. The illustrated readouts span categorical, metric, temporal, and reference-frame queries. Post-training on individual supervision families exposes two challenges. On the one hand, ❶ training can improve its dominant readout while transferring unevenly to other native readouts. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, the categoricalonly control reaches 58.03 on OVO-S but lowers OST from 50.52 to 47.48; trajectory-only training leaves OST nearly flat at 51.03. We use interface lock-in to name this empirical specialization across spatial readouts. The control motivates joint training, while differences in source and task coverage limit attribution to answer format alone (Appendix D.7). On the other hand, ❷ metric or temporal target is valid only under the history that produced it. An observer that moves forward after facing north and one that does so after facing east share the same recent observations and the same local displacement, yet later question about previously seen object has different answers. Supervision that detaches target from its valid prefix can therefore be ambiguous; it is crucial to keep each target attached to the chronological prefix under which it holds. In this paper, we propose ChronoReplay, which consists of two components. First, to address ❶, family-balanced learning keeps every target in its native format (option semantics, units and precision, or timestamp) instead of collapsing it into one canonical answer type, and balances the two families in one objective to regulate their relative influence on the shared model. Second, to address ❷, Causal Replay construction replays both supervision families as chronologically ordered episodes in which every target is attached to the causal prefix under which it is valid, so an accumulated displacement or retrieved timestamp is learned together with the origin and motion that give it meaning (chronological alignment). The main contributions are: We document an empirical interface lock-in pattern (❶): single-family training transfers unevenly across spatial readouts. To address ❶ and ❷, we propose ChronoReplay: family-balanced learning trains all interfaces in their native formats under one objective, and Causal Replay construction keeps every target attached to its chronological prefix. ChronoReplay gains +13.41 OST-Bench, +7.44 UCS-Bench, and +4.91 OVO-S-Bench points under identical observation access, with OVO-S numerically comparable to published 235B reference. Matched interventions show repeatable chronological-order benefit and task-dependent answer-format tradeoff; adaptive frame selection at inference adds separate gain at lower visual cost.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Streaming spatial intelligence. Streaming and long-video models process observations causally and keep history in compressed visual memories, hierarchical summaries, recurrent memory bridges, active response mechanisms, or bounded keyvalue caches [8, 9, 16, 20, 3941, 45, 57, 61, 66, 68, 70, 71]; StreamingBench and OVO-Bench formalize timestamped evaluation under causal access [27, 35], and SimpleStream characterizes the trade-off between recent perception and historical retention [44]. Related memory designs for visual agents include L2-VMAS, which separates perception and thinking into latent memories [67], and AtlasVA, which combines spatial heatmaps, visual exemplars, and symbolic skills to retain visually grounded experience [52]. Spatial benchmarks further require history to stay coherent under object and observer motion and changes of reference frame, from 3D question answering, embodied spatial tests, 2 and long-form egocentric video [1, 13, 33, 34, 50] to multi-view, 4D, and mental-model probes [24, 54]; OVO-S-Bench, OST-Bench, and UCS-Bench extend them to causal streams with categorical, continuous, and timestamp-dependent queries. In this work, we hold observation access fixed and treat it as an orthogonal factor (Section 5.4), and we use these three benchmarks because their answer formats differ; the recipe adds no memory mechanism, and our evaluation covers indoor scenes, so other environments remain untested. Learning reusable spatial representations. Spatial MLLMs acquire geometry through geometry-aware visual features, multi-view or 3D-reconstruction inputs, and large-scale spatial instruction or reinforcement data [4, 14, 28, 36, 38, 60, 73], and persistent spatial state has been represented through 3D scene tokens and embodied generalist agents [17, 19], adaptive fast weights, voxelized allocentric maps, textual scene descriptions, evolving scene graphs, and actionconditioned belief histories [18, 25]. Some mix qualitative and metric spatial questions on single images, and none that we know of asks whether categorical, metric, and temporal formats interfere when one checkpoint is trained on all of them over one causal stream. This is multi-task question: which distinctions does shared representation keep when objectives compete for the same parameters [5, 42, 47, 72], how should their losses be balanced, and what does fine-tuning on one distribution erase from another [22, 32, 69]? Instruction-tuning mixtures raise the same question at the level of data [30, 31, 58], and the answer format itself changes what model appears to know. In sequential state tracking, PAR aligns recurrent predictions with intermediate states to improve length generalization [51]. In this work, we examine the chronology of training episodes and the format and weighting of their targets, and measure the outcome through native benchmarks.

sections.title: 3 Problem Formulation
sections.content: At time model receives the causal observation history ht = (o1, . . . , ot). spatial query arrives with native answer interface κ (a categorical option set, metric value with units, or timestamp), and the VLM predicts zt = fθ(ht), (cid:98)y(κ) = gθ(zt, q, κ), (1) against the task-defined target y(κ) = Aκ(ht, q) Yκ. We call the representation zt reusable over family of query interface pairs when every native target in that family can be read out from the same zt. Reusability is functional requirement, not structural one: the state may stay distributed across the VLM, but histories that lead to different answers must remain distinguishable. Two properties of spatial histories make this demanding. First, interfaces refine one another. categorical target separates spatial regions, whereas metric target for the same quantity resolves variation within region, so representation that keeps only the coarse partition cannot support the finer readout. Second, the state depends on the origin of the history. An observer that moves forward after facing north and one that moves forward after facing east share the same recent observations and the same local displacement, yet later question about previously seen object requires different answers. Histories with identical recent suffixes but different origins must therefore map to different states. Our goal is to learn one fθ with both properties from heterogeneous native supervision; Section 4 builds training episodes that expose both.

sections.title: 4.1 Overview
sections.content: ChronoReplay post-trains VLM so that one shared representation supports native spatial readouts while preserving the history each readout depends on. Figure 2 summarizes two stages. Causal Replay construction forms the replay pool: every target is kept in its native format and every episode is ordered chronologically. Family-balanced learning normalizes the single-turn preservation and metrictemporal trajectory risks, then controls their relative contribution to the shared parameters. Algorithm 1 in Appendix lists both stages.

sections.title: 4.3 Family-Balanced Learning
sections.content: Motivation. What if the two families differ in size? With targets and histories fixed, the remaining choice is how much each family may move the shared parameters. The preservation family DP holds 33,180 single-turn examples (30,635 categorical and 2,545 numerical), whereas the trajectory family DT holds 6,381 ordered episodes (45,006 supervised metric, counting, judgement, and temporal turns). Raw row counts could let one family dominate the shared parameters and reproduce ❶ inside joint training. Therefore, we normalize risk within each family and set their ratio explicitly rather than learning it [10, 21]. Family risks. Let ℓP be the native loss for preservation example r, with source-defined weight wr (Appendix C). ChronoReplay combines the risks as Lreplay = (1 λ) LP + λ LT , λ = α 1 + α , where α is trajectory loss mass relative to preservation. We use α = 0.5 in the main experiments: trajectory receives 1/3 of total mass; preservation receives 2/3, split equally between categorical and numerical targets. sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: In this section, we evaluate ChronoReplay from multiple perspectives and organize the analysis around four research questions. RQ1: Does ChronoReplay transfer across categorical, continuous, and timestamp-causal benchmarks under fixed observation access (Section 5.2)? RQ2: How do single-family and joint training transfer across spatial readouts (Section 5.3)? RQ3: Which components carry the effect: native formats, chronological order, or family mass (Section 5.3)? RQ4: How much of the OVO-S system score is observation access rather than training (Section 5.4)? 5 (5) (6)

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate on three benchmarks: OVO-S-Bench tests categorical reasoning on egocentric perception, object permanence, and allocentric mapping [23]; OST-Bench scores agent state, visible information, temporal localization, counting, and agentobject relations over multi-round exploration [26]; and UCS-Bench has 8,114 timestamp-causal questions on trajectories, pose, proximity, object identity, and quantity [56]. All checkpoints start from the same official Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct revision [2]. ChronoReplay trains the language model and visual merger (visual encoder frozen) on the 33,180-sequence preservation family and the 6,381-episode trajectory family with α = 0.5, and canonical scene identities keep every test scene out of training. The single-family diagnostic compares CATEGORICAL-ONLY and TRAJECTORY-ONLY variants with full ChronoReplay (Appendix D.7). Its categorical-only arm is distinct from the main preservation pool, which also contains numerical targets. SHIFTED cyclically rotates the turn blocks of every episode while keeping their content, controlling for chronological alignment; CANONICAL rewrites every target as typed value field, controlling for native formats (the ChronoReplay default is NATIVE); and Uniform-81 matches the average frame count of adaptive access, an equal-cost control for observation access. Model-only comparisons hold causal observation access fixed (OVO-S Uniform-128, the complete scene-disjoint OST protocol, all UCS questions), while adaptive access (Appendix E) is an inference-time policy applied separately to the same checkpoint. Published models are reference points under their own protocols, and mechanism claims rely on matched Qwen3-VL-8B comparisons. Appendix lists optimization settings, matched controls, and four-GPU replication.

We call the uneven cross-readout transfer observed in single-family training interface lock-in, an empirical pattern rather than an isolated internal mechanism. The singlefamily comparison retains the tradeoff: categorical-only training favors OVO-S, trajectory-only training gives little OST Overall gain, and full ChronoReplay has the highest three-benchmark mean. Objective controls show further gains beyond ordinary joint SFT. The full recipe gains 13.41 OST points over the base; the paired cyclic-shift control isolates smaller, repeatable 2.41-point contribution from preserving source chronology as whole. Native and canonical answer formats redistribute gains across UCS and OST rather than establishing universally best encoding. OVO-S improves across all four levels, including +5.01 points on L4, which remains the hardest subset. These findings support ChronoReplay as simple recipe for balanced cross-interface transfer without assigning its full gain to one component or claiming dominance on every spatial subcategory.

sections.title: AI use statement
sections.content: Generative AI was used in two roles. AI assistants supported literature search, research brainstorming, manuscript revision, code editing, debugging, and data-pipeline implementation. In upstream data preparation, multimodal teachers were also used for bounded tasks such as proposing linguistic forms or assessing whether source evidence was visible and answerable. These teachers did not define spatial ground truth, and protected evaluation labels, predictions, and scores were unavailable to data construction. Every target used by ChronoReplay is bound to source annotation, deterministic geometry, simulator state, or an audited public label; reported results are produced by frozen benchmark scorers. The authors designed the research, checked AI-assisted code, citations, claims, and prose against source papers and versioned experimental records, and take responsibility for the complete work.

sections.title: Ethics statement
sections.content: This work uses existing research datasets and public benchmarks; it recruits no human participants and collects no new video or indoor scans. Source media may contain identifiable people, private-like interiors, or contextual information. Any artifact release therefore follows the corresponding source licenses and does not redistribute benchmark media. Canonical scene isolation prevents reported evaluation scenes and labels from entering training. Streaming spatial models may nevertheless inherit demographic, geographic, and environmental biases from their source data, and their ability to retain people, objects, and locations over time could enable surveillance or unsafe embodied decisions. We have not audited these high-stakes uses and do not claim suitability for surveillance, autonomous navigation, or other safety-critical deployment.

sections.title: Reproducibility statement
sections.content: Appendices BD specify the evaluation contracts, replay data, scene isolation, chronological construction, optimization, and controlled comparisons. Appendix separately specifies the fixed-parameter observation-access intervention, and Appendix records the executable configurations, generation parameters, scorer contracts, and source manifests. Every retained trainable comparison starts independently from the same pinned public Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct revision; no intermediate checkpoint continuation or model fusion is used. Reported OVO-S, OST, and UCS scores bind model, data, protocol, prediction, and scorer identities, and all reported values are defined once as macros in main.tex and traced to versioned result records. Code, configurations, frozen training-selection manifests, and scoring scripts are available at the code repository; the project homepage provides the paper and an overview of the released resources. Model weights and converted training annotations are available through single Hugging Face collection. The data release preserves the frozen sample order, native targets, training weights, and supervision masks; raw media and saved predictions are not bundled. Releasing the accepted records makes reproducing the reported training mixture independent of re-querying any external AI service.

A.3 What Family Balance Does and Does Not Control Proposition 3 (Invariances of the balanced objective). Let LP and LT be the family risks of Eq. 5 and Lreplay = (1 λ)LP + λLT with λ = α/(1 + α). sections.content: B.1 Attribution Framework Performance depends jointly on the trained model and its observation access. Let J(θ, π) denote benchmark performance with model parameters θ and observation policy π. We separate the two effects as train = J(θ, π0) J(θ0, π0), access = J(θ, π1) J(θ, π0), (9) where θ0 is the official base model, θ is the model trained with ChronoReplay, π0 is the standard observation policy, and π1 is adaptive access (Appendix E). The first contrast changes the trained model under identical observation access. The second changes observation access while holding the model parameters fixed. The complete system evaluates J(θ, π1), while the two controlled contrasts separate the training and access effects. We examine design choices through matched training interventions. The origin-shift intervention preserves the same multiset of turn blocks and supervision weights while changing their episode-level chronology and the accumulated context preceding each target. Initialization and optimization settings are held fixed. The target-interface experiment changes the answer representation while preserving the causal histories and training configuration. These comparisons probe sensitivity to the corresponding design choices of ChronoReplay. 18 B.2 Benchmark Protocols OVO-S-Bench. We retain the evaluated boundary convention = max(1, tq), with frame indices starting at zero. The benchmark timestamps place this boundary within the video. Local and global coverage. Global sampling takes the integer floors of 128 equally spaced positions on the inclusive interval [0, e], then sorts and removes repeated indices. Local sampling uses spacing = max(1, round(f /4)) and the index sequence Ilocal = {max(0, 7d), max(0, 7d) + d, . . . , e}, (13) retaining the final eight indices if rounding produces an extra sample. Multiscale coverage. With budget = 128, the most recent 30 seconds receive round(0.6B) samples. The preceding interval extending to 300 seconds before the query receives round(0.3B) samples, and the remaining budget covers the earlier history. Define s30 = max(0, 30f ) and s300 = max(0, 300f ). Let Lin(a, b, n) return the integer floors of equally spaced positions in [a, b). The requested indices are Imulti = Lin(s30, e, round(0.6B)) Lin(s300, s30, round(0.3B)) Lin(0, s300, nearly), (14) where nearly is the remaining budget. Empty intervals are skipped and repeated indices are removed. Global and local sampling include the query boundary; multiscale intervals exclude their right endpoint. These conventions preserve the sampling procedure used for the reported results. The official model improves from 48.98 to 54.08, while ChronoReplay improves from 53.89 to 57.98 under our fixed OVO-S evaluation protocol. Each comparison holds the model parameters fixed and varies the observations presented at inference. The comparison at similar frame budget further examines temporal placement. Uniform sampling of 81 positions from the ordered set of 128 uniform indices obtains 52.40, whereas adaptive selection obtains 57.98 using 80.50 frames on average. The advantage of 5.58 points supports matching temporal coverage to query scope at approximately the same visual cost. Figures are selected examples of output differences; they do not estimate the prevalence of errors or identify an observation-selection failure. Figures 57 use Run 2 of Table 12. Two additional cases examine native supervision complementarity and global-layout failure. The first uses the historical diagnostic models specified in Appendix F.4; the second compares Base and the headline ChronoReplay model under fixed observations. F.1 Historical State Retrieval Figure 4 illustrates how an earlier state supports both temporal answer and later reference-relative displacement. The retrieval question requires the round in which the two objects occupied the specified side of the observer. The outputs distinguish recovery of that earlier state from selection of later observation. 26 Figure 4: Historical context in spatial reasoning. The second answer depends on interpreting later observations in the specified reference frame. OVO-S uses greedy answer generation with the fixed evaluation prompt and deterministic answer extraction, an eight-token ceiling, and batch size two. OST uses greedy decoding with temperature 0, top-p = 1, one sample, and 512 tokens; UCS uses temperature 0, one sample, and eight tokens. No voting, prompt ensemble, or benchmark-dependent parameter choice contributes to paper row. 37 I.2 Data and Media Audits All training examples are bound to canonical scene identities and source annotations before optimization. The same data separation is applied to the main model and every matched control. Complete media, row, and scene manifests are retained with the released configuration. Each release binds row hashes, counts, family mass, supervised turns, and the media manifest. Every referenced image and video is decoded and audited once before training: items at or above the 32,768-token limit or above the declared visual-pixel budget are rejected, and isolation audits bind canonical physical scenes. I.3 Scorer and Manifest Contracts Each reported result binds the model, observations, predictions, annotations, and scoring protocol. Evaluation follows the fixed OVO-S protocol in Appendix B, the fixed 8,351-turn OST manifest, and all 8,114 UCS questions. Result records and source manifests link every evaluation identity to the values defined in main.tex and will be released with the code. Native responses are passed to the unchanged task scorer. For canonical responses, frozen reader extracts the leading typed value field from the generated response alone and supplies that value to the same scorer; it does not inspect the question, task identity, reference answer, label, or score. All 8,351 OST responses and all 8,114 UCS responses yield an extracted value. The official OST scorer evaluates its designated 7,814 turns.
